extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR managers, counselors, and educators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for professional conduct, accountability, accreditation, and societal responsibility in public relations practice, aimed at helping practitioners and students judge and improve ethical and professional performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional Privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals hold privileged positions because of trust inherent in fiduciary relationships and because their specialized knowledge and skills are valuable; they must commit to uphold the profession by honoring its obligations and values (e.g., the Hippocratic Oath obligates physicians to work for the benefit, not harm, of patients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionals must invest time and effort to acquire knowledge and skills and must avoid violating fiduciary relationships or exploiting clients; such violations threaten client welfare and public trust in the profession. Protection of clients and the profession includes establishing codes of ethics and standards of practice, often backed by law or state sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Responsibility of Public Relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations must fulfill moral obligations to society by considering the welfare of the larger society when helping clients solve problems and by acting as a collective moral agent for societal betterment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations' value is enhanced when it (1) promotes free, ethical competition of ideas and information, (2) reveals sources and goals of participants, and (3) enforces high standards of conduct. Value is diminished when it (1) suppresses competition of ideas, (2) hides true sources of PR efforts, or (3) leaves unethical or incompetent practice unchallenged. Practitioners should consider societal impacts (example: a guerrilla marketing stunt that caused public panic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Positives — Socially Responsible PR Adds Public Value
rubrics_metrics.description: Five major positives of socially responsible public relations: (1) improves professional practice via codified ethics and standards; (2) improves organizational conduct by emphasizing need for public approval; (3) serves public interest by making varied viewpoints articulate; (4) serves segmented society by replacing misinformation with information and discord with rapport; (5) promotes human welfare by helping social systems adapt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria justify PR's public value — e.g., fundraising for public goods, campaigns to address public health and social problems, reducing discrimination, and fostering global understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negatives — Ways PR Can Harm Public Communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Three major negatives: (1) PR promotes special interests sometimes at the cost of public well-being; (2) publicity clutters communication channels with pseudo-events and phony phrases that confuse; (3) PR can corrode communication with cynicism and credibility gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should avoid obfuscation and obscuring complex public issues; be vigilant about creating noise that undermines credibility. Historical critiques (e.g., Heilbroner) illustrate how overuse of publicity can cheapen trust in genuine behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes of Ethics as a Professional Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Adherence to a set of professional norms—codes of ethics—is a basic requirement for professions; codes may be established by employers or professional associations (e.g., PRSA, IABC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codes provide criteria to guide and judge behavior but are effective only with commitment, training, and enforcement. A code alone may be merely 'window dressing' unless organizations accept and apply it. The PRSA Code has evolved from enforcement to education (PRSA examples and history cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement Mechanisms and Limitations (PRSA example)
rubrics_metrics.description: PRSA members agree to conduct professional lives according to the code; compliance is enforced via confidential proceedings by an eleven-member national Board of Ethics and Professional Standards which investigates complaints and recommends sanctions, including membership revocation or expulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement has been uneven: few cases referred, many dismissed for lack of evidence, settled, or rendered moot by resignation/death. A key limitation is that the PRSA code applies only to members, reducing reach and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer Adoption, Training, and Contractual Commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers and firms can institutionalize ethical practice by training staff, supporting employees who refuse unethical client requests, and requiring employees to sign agreements to practice according to PRSA or firm codes even when not PRSA members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: firms holding regular ethics training on conflicts of interest, transparency about client relationships, disclosure when speaking for paying clients, and company policies that protect employees who object to unethical requests. Such institutional support is crucial to making codes meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual Moral Responsibility and Common Pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate responsibility for ethical decision making rests with individual practitioners, who must be prepared to evaluate dilemmas using professional codes and moral reasoning. A common pitfall is assuming 'if it isn't illegal, it must be all right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethics require more than legal compliance; practitioners must exercise moral judgment. Training and moral development are often more useful in practice than codes alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability via Occupational Licensure — Legal Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensure as a mechanism for accountability raises constitutional and practical issues: freedom of expression (First Amendment), states' rights to regulate occupations (Tenth Amendment), and individuals' right to pursue occupations. Licensure must be justified by a compelling state interest to regulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. courts have been skeptical that controversy or potential for abuse justifies licensure; licensing to professionalize practice has no automatic legal basis. Advocates propose voluntary licensing limited to using the label 'licensed public relations practitioner' rather than restricting speech or employment, but licensure faces legal and practical obstacles and is unlikely to be imposed soon in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation as an Alternative to Licensing (APR, ABC examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accreditation (e.g., APR by Universal Accreditation Board; ABC by IABC) offers voluntary credentialing: portfolio presentation, panel interview, rigorous computer test; maintenance via continuing education points (e.g., APR requires 10 points every three years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accreditation can raise standards, improve salaries, link PR work to organizational goals, and indicate commitment to ethical practice. However, multiple accreditation bodies and lack of a single consolidated certification weaken claims of professional uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical Differences Between Accredited and Unaccredited Practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies find accredited practitioners tend to be older, have more experience, higher education, higher salaries, report to higher management, and engage more in strategic planning and ethics/legal issues than non-APRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These differences support accreditation's value but do not guarantee employer preference; many employers still do not require accreditation or PR education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Gaining Professional Acceptance and Stature
rubrics_metrics.description: To be accepted as a true profession, PR needs standardized educational curriculum, a research-based body of knowledge, enforceable codes of ethics, and uniform accountability processes; current gaps (easy entry, ignorance of theory, codes limited to members, fragmented accreditation) hinder full professional status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners who combine ethics, commitment, knowledge, and skills will distinguish PR as a calling serving public interest. Institutional and cultural change (education, consolidation of accreditation) is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of Ethics and Competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionalism requires both ethical conduct and functional competence; ethics without competence is meaningless; competence without ethics is directionless and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must cultivate both moral judgment and technical skill. Quoted guidance: 'Ethics and expertise belong together; only together do they constitute true professionalism.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Case/Discussion Situations to Apply Codes (Exhibit 5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical ethical dilemmas (e.g., disclosure of confidential proposal information; publishing optimistic forecasts without disclosure of client relationship or negative facts; creating secretly financed 'independent' citizens' organizations; delivering speeches containing false claims) should be resolved by referring to professional codes (IABC, PRSA) and ethical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit 5.6 provides concrete scenarios to practice applying codes of ethics and to train moral reasoning; recommended to use as discussion/training prompts in ethics education.
